name: swe-sim
description: Turns underspecified GitHub issues into graded coding-agent tasks with a simulated stakeholder and hidden tests

readme.html:
swe-sim

swe-sim turns underspecified GitHub issues into graded tasks for coding agents. The agent gets the issue as its reporter wrote it and a simulated stakeholder it may ask about what is missing. It submits a patch, and hidden tests in a separate offline container grade it. Each task runs in three conditions against one frozen reward contract, so you can measure what asking is worth. A task enters the pool only after a set of executed controls shows its grader cannot be fooled by a no-op, a wrong patch or a tampered test run.

The Python package and the CLI are both named swesim.

The idea

Many SWE-bench issues are underspecified: the information that settled them is in the discussion thread and the fix, not in the issue. swe-sim keeps the issue as the brief. It moves the missing information into a ledger of facts, each quoted from the thread or the fix, and gives the stakeholder those facts. The stakeholder speaks as the reporter. It describes the behaviour wanted and observed, and never the tests, the oracle or which of the agent's options to pick.

Condition What the agent sees
full The natural brief plus every stakeholder-visible fact
hidden The selected brief only: the natural issue, or a withheld version with recorded spans removed
interactive The same brief as hidden, plus ask-user and confirm-behavior to reach the stakeholder

All three conditions share one contract. The FAIL_TO_PASS tests are split into weighted requirement groups. The reward is partial credit over those groups, and any PASS_TO_PASS regression sets it to zero. success means the whole contract passed. Asking changes what the agent knows, never the tests or the weights.

Grading happens in a separate offline container. A root-owned collector freezes the submitted tree and the stakeholder transcript. The verifier diffs the tree against the untouched base and drops edits to protected paths (contract tests, pytest configuration, conftest and startup hooks, package metadata). It then runs the hidden tests and requires the collected test ids, JUnit, the terminal summary and the exit status to agree. The full contract is in docs/grading.md.

A drafted task must pass nine code-owned approval gates: schema, asset hashes, judge acceptance, a load-bearing on-request fact, grounded requirements, withholding leaks, exact brief reconstruction, controls present, and fact scope. It then must pass executed controls before it can be registered:

Control Must show
No-op Reward 0; the FAIL_TO_PASS tests fail on the base and the PASS_TO_PASS tests hold
Oracle (the real fix) Success 1 and reward 1
Plausible-wrong patch Applies, fails correctness, stays under its declared reward ceiling
Tamper (root conftest.py, sitecustomize.py, skip marker) Applies and earns exactly 0 without an infrastructure failure
Reachability probe The gold commit and distinctive post-fix lines cannot be reached from the agent's environment

How a task is made and run

flowchart LR
  A["Repository URL or SWE-bench pool"] --> B["Discover and judge"]
  B --> C["Probe base and gold on Modal"]
  C --> D["Draft facts and briefs"]
  D --> E["Approval gates"]
  E --> F["Compile and validate controls"]
  F --> G["Register"]
  G --> H["Run through Temporal"]
  H --> I["Grade, audit, score and export"]
Loading

Tasks come from two sources: the human-annotated SWE-bench Verified pool, and any GitHub repository URL, where discovery finds merged PRs with linked issues and filters them by diff size. Tasks are compiled to Harbor 0.23 task directories, and Harbor builds and runs both images on Modal. The agent is mini-swe-agent, running as an unprivileged user with a host allowlist; the verifier has no network. Temporal orchestrates creation and trials. The hosted deployment consists of four Cloud Run worker pools, one Cloud Run Job per trial, a versioned GCS bucket as the record, a Cloud SQL index and an IAP-protected console (docs/architecture.md).

Run it locally

You need Python 3.12 and uv. The offline suite needs no credentials, no Docker and no network after the first sync:

uv sync --extra dev --frozen
uv run --frozen --offline python -m pytest -q tests --ignore=tests/integration
uv run --frozen swesim --help

tests/test_compile.py::test_llm_helpers expects OPENAI_API_KEY to be absent. If your shell exports it, run the suite under env -u OPENAI_API_KEY. The tests under tests/integration need live credentials.

You can inspect the tracked example offline as well. These commands check every file against the example's manifest and recompute one run's reward from the verifier's per-test observations (examples/README.md walks through each file):

uv run --frozen python -c "
import hashlib, json, pathlib
root = pathlib.Path('examples/mwaskom--seaborn-3190'); m = json.load(open(root / 'manifest.json'))
bad = [p for p, h in m['files'].items() if hashlib.sha256((root / p).read_bytes()).hexdigest() != h]
print('ok' if not bad else bad)"

To create and run tasks yourself you need a Modal account, model-provider keys (Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter, per the roles you configure), a GitHub token for mining and a Temporal namespace. Configuration lives in a git-ignored .env generated from .env.example, which explains every variable. The supported deployment is the hosted one: docs/setup.md goes from an empty GCP project to a running pipeline in seven checked steps, and docs/runbook.md covers operations. scripts/vm/ keeps an older single-VM backend with a local Temporal dev server.

Results

Every number below comes from a file in this repository. The sample sizes are small, so treat them as measurements of the pipeline, not as claims about models.

The tracked example passes its controls. examples/mwaskom--seaborn-3190/validation.json records the controls that admitted SWE-bench instance mwaskom__seaborn-3190. The no-op scored reward 0 (FAIL_TO_PASS 0 of 1, PASS_TO_PASS 84 of 84). The oracle scored reward 1. The plausible-wrong patch scored 0. Each of the three tamper patches scored 0 with a protected-path-edit signal. The reachability probe found no gold-commit hits. The three tracked runs, two interactive and one hidden, each scored reward 1.0 with 85 of 85 tests passing (runs/*/reward.json). In one interactive run the agent asked one question, got a behaviour-level answer and had its fix confirmed. The hidden run passed too, so on this task the model did not need the stakeholder.

The first hosted task found a task-authoring defect. On pytest-dev--pytest-7283, 29 hosted trials cost $3.01 in total: four models, three conditions, k=2, plus a screen and a demonstration run. Two models solved every condition (7 of 7 and 6 of 6). For the other two, scores ran the wrong way: full < hidden < interactive (0/3, 3/5, 2/2 and 0/2, 1/2, 2/2). The cause was a stakeholder-visible fact that described behaviour only a PASS_TO_PASS test covered. Agents given every fact acted on it, and one regressed a passing test. The fix was a ninth approval gate, fact-scope, which rejects such a fact. The per-cell table, costs and caveats are in docs/grading.md.

The issue judge is weak on recall. The judge decides which issues count as underspecified. Against the human labels on 145 annotated SWE-bench rows, openai/gpt-5.5 scored agreement 0.655, precision 0.644 and recall 0.460, and anthropic/claude-opus-5 scored 0.634, 0.604 and 0.460. Answering "not underspecified" every time would score 82/145 = 0.566 on the same rows (from the confusion counts in docs/grading.md). The judge misses more than half of the underspecified issues.

Earlier runs, kept separate. registry.json lists three version-2 scenarios. Their 19 current-spec trials scored 6/6 on seaborn, 7/7 on scikit-learn and 0/6 on pypdf. The saved task-sense audit flags the pypdf hidden test as unfair: it calls a helper that only the oracle introduces. So that 0/6 shows a task defect, not difficulty (docs/grading.md).

Limits. Submitted code runs inside pytest's process and can try to forge its reports. The four-way evidence check catches disagreement, but it does not prove isolation. The stakeholder's reporter stance is partly prompt-enforced and is measured by a disclosure audit. Interactive episodes stay unadjudicated until a person reviews them.

Repository map

  • swesim/: models, stages (mine, judge, draft, approve, compile, validate, run, score, export), sources, verifier, stakeholder service, Temporal workflows, index and console.
  • tests/: the offline suite; tests/integration/ needs credentials.
  • examples/mwaskom--seaborn-3190/: a sanitized, hash-listed snapshot of one validated task and three runs.
  • infra/, Dockerfile.worker, cloudbuild.yaml, scripts/cloud/: hosted infrastructure and deployment.
  • docs/: architecture, grading, setup, runbook, operations record; docs/superpowers/ holds the design specs and plans, and docs/reviews/ holds adversarial reviews of the design.
  • data/annotations/: OpenAI's SWE-bench Verified annotations, which the SWE-bench source and the judge calibration read, plus two pool subsets derived from them.
